transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-07-21 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Nebula Head of Platform), Liam O'Connor (Nebula SRE), Jordan Miles (Nebula CTO)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Redwood walked through Console and API controls for multi-tenant rate limiting, org vs project key patterns, burst capacity, and how Dedicated / Hosted modes interact with quota policies. Customer asked about data residency, KMS encryption, and how to limit noisy tenants. Next steps: follow-up perf test, share security docs, pricing.

Topics covered:
- Org/project key hierarchy and routing semantics
- Quotas: concurrency, token, and request-per-minute slices
- Burst capacity and graceful fallback between variants
- Console UI for policies and fairshare simulator
- Security: SSO, audit logs, KMS integration

Action items called out during meeting (captured in metadata too):
- Maya to send playbook and pricing
- Diego to run perf spike test
- Priya to share tenant usage patterns

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya Chen from Redwood, AE on the account. Diego and I will run through a short console and API demo focused on tenant controls.
[00:18] Jordan Miles: Thanks, Maya. We have about 30-ish minutes for the demo, then a bit of time for Q&A. We're particularly worried about noisy neighbors — one of our products had a spike yesterday and it knocked over some shared endpoints.
[00:35] Diego Ramirez: Yeah totally, that's exactly what we're aiming to show — org vs project key patterns, and how you can carve quotas so that one tenant can't starve others. I'll jump into the console in a sec.
[00:48] Priya Rao: Quick context — we're running a hybrid setup: most inference sits in our VPC using your Private offering, but we also use Hosted for dev traffic. We care about per-tenant SLAs and need audit trails for compliance.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Got it. That hybrid mix makes sense. We'll show both API-level keying and Console policies so you can see how it maps to Dedicated/Private. Diego, screenshare ready?
[01:20] Diego Ramirez: Yep, sharing now. You might see a slight lag on screen share, bear with me.
[01:32] [01:32] Diego Ramirez: Alright, this is the Redwood Console. Top-left is the Projects view, top-right is an org-level policy panel. Quick note: our terminology sometimes gets munged in transcripts — we say "org key" to mean the top-level key tied to billing and broad quotas, and "project key" to mean per-application tokens within that org.
[01:58] Liam O'Connor: Are project keys namespaced under a project? We have teams who want separate billing but same org.
[02:07] Diego Ramirez: Yes, you can nest project keys under projects. You can also pin projects to different capacity pools — for example, reserve Dedicated GPUs for high-SLA projects and let dev projects burst to hosted.
[02:25] Jordan Miles: How do routing and fallback work in that case? If Dedicated is saturated, does traffic fail or shift to hosted?
[02:34] Diego Ramirez: Good question. There are routing policies: preferred route, fallback route, and cost-priority route. If Dedicated is full, a request can fall back to a compatible model in Hosted with a lower SLA, or you can configure automatic queueing/backpressure. We also support rate guard policies to reject outright if you want hard limits.
[02:55] Priya Rao: What about token counting? We have variable prompt lengths, sometimes very long. We need predictable billing and SLOs.
[03:07] Maya Chen: We expose token usage both at org and project key levels; the Console shows rolling histograms. Also our Optimize tool will recommend batching and KV cache tuning to reduce per-token unit cost for long-context workloads.
[03:22] [03:22] Diego Ramirez: I'm going to demo creating a quota policy. So we click Policies -> Create -> Rate Policy. Here you can set concurrency, requests-per-minute, and token ceilings. For multi-tenant fairness we recommend a fairshare slice per project key so every active key gets a weighted share.
[03:43] Liam O'Connor: Weighted share — can you do dynamic weight adjustments? Some tenants pay more and should get priority during congestion.
[03:53] Diego Ramirez: Yes, you can set priority tiers. During congestion the fairshare allocator uses weights; higher-weight tenants get proportionally more capacity. There's also a preemption flag that can preempt lower-tier requests if necessary.
[04:06] Jordan Miles: Any built-in visibility for which tenant is being throttled? We need to alert product owners.
[04:15] Diego Ramirez: Each throttled request emits an audit event with key id, policy id, and reason; those feed into Console graphs and you can forward them to your SIEM. The event includes approximate latency, queue time, and token counts.
[04:29] Priya Rao: You mentioned KV cache — does that persist across project keys? We've seen some leakage when reusing caches.
[04:40] Diego Ramirez: By default KV cache is isolated per model instance and per tenant, but you can configure shared prefixes if you want reuse between internal projects. We advise isolating customer tenants. The Console shows cache hit rates by project key.
[04:57] [04:57] Maya Chen: Quick interjection on compliance — for Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS/HSM, support SAML/SSO for RBAC, and keep audit logs in your control plane. Diego, maybe show the security panel briefly?
[05:12] Diego Ramirez: Sure. In the org settings you can toggle encryption-at-rest with your KMS, configure SAML mappings to groups for role-based access, and set log retention policies for audit trails. There's an option to push logs to your S3 bucket in the VPC.
[05:30] Liam O'Connor: That S3 push — is it agentless or do we run a collector?
[05:36] Diego Ramirez: It's agentless for Private deployments — we write to a pre-authorized bucket via a cross-account role. For on-prem we support a small collector if you want to keep data completely internal.
[05:47] [05:47] Jordan Miles: Ok, show us an example policy that prevents a runaway job from consuming all tokens.
[05:54] Diego Ramirez: Creating a policy now. We'll set a per-project token ceiling of 2M tokens per hour, concurrency 10, rpm 1200. Then we attach it at the org level with an override for three high-SLA project keys. The Console allows policy inheritance and overrides so you can centralize control.
[06:18] Priya Rao: If a project hits token ceiling mid-run, do we see partial completions? We need predictable failures not silent truncation.
[06:28] Diego Ramirez: We surface a 429-like response with an explicit reason code; the SDKs map it to a Retry-After or a short-circuit depending on your retry policy. There's also a streaming fallback where the model can finish generation in hosted but with lower throughput.
[06:44] Maya Chen: Important: the SDK and API error codes are documented; we also provide sample middleware to map retries to exponential backoff tuned for token budgets.
[06:55] [06:55] Liam O'Connor: Let's talk billing implications — if we move traffic to Hosted as fallback, do we get double-billed?
[07:04] Maya Chen: No double billing. If traffic is routed to Hosted, the org/project that initiated the request is billed according to the model variant used. If you reserve Dedicated capacity, that reservation covers Dedicated usage; fallback into Hosted is billed separately. We can model those scenarios in the cost estimator.
[07:21] Jordan Miles: Can we do a dry-run to simulate a noisy tenant?
[07:26] Diego Ramirez: Yes, the Console has a Fairness Simulator. I'll open it: you can inject synthetic traffic patterns per key. I'm going to simulate a 10x spike on a dev key.
[07:40] [07:40] Diego Ramirez: Running the sim — you can see the fairshare allocator rebalancing. The dev key hits its burst window, then gets throttled to preserve high-SLA keys. There's a trace view you can click to see which policy fired.
[07:58] Priya Rao: Nice; can we export that trace to our incident system?
[08:04] Diego Ramirez: Yep, export as JSON or push to your webhook/SIEM.
[08:10] [08:10] Jordan Miles: On the technical side, we need to ensure the rate limiter scales horizontally. Does the limiter become a single point of failure?
[08:20] Diego Ramirez: It's distributed — we shard the allocator by token namespace and use eventual consistency for counters with per-node local buffering to avoid hot shards. In very tight tail-latency scenarios we fall back to a centralized guard, but that path is rare and instrumented.
[08:38] Liam O'Connor: Sharding by namespace — what is the namespace key? Is it the org id or project id?
[08:45] Diego Ramirez: Namespace is by project key by default but you can configure org-level slicing if that's a better fit for your topology.
[08:55] [08:55] Priya Rao: Security question — do audit logs contain full prompt text? We have PII concerns.
[09:04] Maya Chen: By default we redact prompts in audit events. You can enable full-text logging if you have a Private deployment and control retention; otherwise we send redacted metadata.
[09:16] Jordan Miles: Good. Also, does Redwood Optimize recommend quantization for models? We want lower cost for low-criticality tenants.
[09:25] Diego Ramirez: Yes, Optimize will suggest model family and quantization profiles based on your workload patterns. You can map those suggestions to specific project keys, so low-cost tenants go to a quantized variant automatically.
[09:37] [09:37] Priya Rao: What's the uplift / downgrade path? If quantized variant quality regresses we want automatic rollback.
[09:44] Diego Ramirez: We support canary rollouts with evaluation hooks. You can define a prompt set and quality thresholds; if metrics drop we automatically fall back to previous model. Rollouts are tied to model versions, so you can pin critical tenants to a stable variant.
[09:58] Maya Chen: Quick pause: any legal/procurement blockers we should be aware of?
[10:04] Jordan Miles: We'll need data residency statements for EU and US, plus SOC 2 evidence. Procurement also asks about indemnities but that comes later.
[10:14] Maya Chen: We'll include SOC 2 summary and a network diagram in the follow-up.
[10:20] [10:20] Liam O'Connor: A nit — we saw older Redwood docs refer to "KV-cache" as shared; typo'd it 'K V cache' in a doc and engineers got confused.
[10:30] Diego Ramirez: We get that. We'll send a short FAQ with terminology.
[10:34] [10:34] Diego Ramirez: I'm going to switch to the API demo quickly. Here's a sample request using an org key and project key header: Authorization: Bearer org_XXXXX; X-Project-Key: proj_YYYYY. You can also pass routing hints in the X-Route header for preferred capacity.
[10:56] Priya Rao: Can keys be rotated automatically without downtime?
[11:01] Diego Ramirez: Yes, key rotation supports a grace window. You can upload the new key and set a rollover period; requests present either key during the transition.
[11:11] Jordan Miles: Does Redwood support multiple project keys per service? We have microservices that call through a shared gateway.
[11:18] Maya Chen: You can mint project keys per service and bind them to roles. We also support token scoping so a gateway can exchange a long-lived org key for short-lived scoped project tokens.
[11:31] [11:31] Liam O'Connor: Ok show us the logs for a throttled request.
[11:36] Diego Ramirez: Here's an example event: {timestamp, key_id, policy_id, reason: 'rate_limit_exceeded', approximate_tokens, queue_time_ms}. The console shows a human-friendly message and a link to the raw JSON.
[11:52] Priya Rao: Slight concern — we have GDPR regs. If logs contain keys, how do we redact?
[11:59] Maya Chen: We can hash key ids in logs or keep mapping tables in your VPC; for Private deployments we recommend the hashed approach and local mapping so you control full key->tenant mappings.
[12:14] [12:14] Jordan Miles: Any recommended starting policy for teams like ours with mixed production/dev workloads?
[12:21] Diego Ramirez: A common pattern: org-level baseline quota, per-project fairshare slices, and a dev burst bucket with lower priority. Reserve Dedicated for top 5 revenue tenants, allow dev to burst to Hosted but cap tokens per-day. We'll include a playbook.
[12:38] Maya Chen: Let's talk about pricing briefly — pricing differs by model family and deployment. We'll model a scenario where 60% of traffic hits Dedicated and 40% falls back to Hosted during spikes; that changes monthly cost.
[12:53] Jordan Miles: Can you send an estimate? We'll need it for our finance review.
[12:59] Maya Chen: Yes — action: I'll send a cost model with the playbook.
[13:04] [13:04] Diego Ramirez: One more demo: jitter and backpressure. If a tenant floods requests we apply leaky-bucket smoothing at the edge and queue for up to a configurable window; beyond that we return a policy-coded 429. Here I configure a 10s max queue.
[13:23] Priya Rao: For streaming responses, does queueing affect streaming latency?
[13:28] Diego Ramirez: It can. For streaming we prioritize starting the stream quickly; queueing affects when that stream begins. We expose queue_time in headers so you can instrument.
[13:39] [13:39] Jordan Miles: Ok we've seen enough for the demo. A few follow-up questions: 1) Can you run a spike test on our traces? 2) What's the timeline for pilot? 3) What's SLA for Dedicated?
[13:50] Maya Chen: 1) Yes Diego will run that — action item. 2) Pilot timeline depends on infra — typical pilot is 4-6 weeks for Private, 2-3 for Hosted/Dedicated initial commit. 3) SLA for Dedicated is 99.95% uptime and latency SLOs by model family; we'll share exact numbers.
[14:12] Priya Rao: One more — on audit retention, we need 1 year of immutable logs for some products. Is that supported?
[14:20] Diego Ramirez: Yes, we can push immutable logs to your archive S3 with object lock for retention. That works for Private or Dedicated with retained control.
[14:33] Maya Chen: Great. Any blockers on next steps?
[14:37] Jordan Miles: No blockers. We'll get the token histograms and list of tenants.
[14:42] Priya Rao: We'll also need the SOC 2 summary and network diagram to share with procurement.
[14:48] Maya Chen: We'll include both.
[14:51] Liam O'Connor: Quick note — can we do the perf run with 14:00–16:00 PST window? That's our low-traffic window.
[14:58] Diego Ramirez: We'll coordinate dates but that works.
[15:03] Maya Chen: Awesome. If there's nothing else we can wrap. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and set the perf test.
[15:12] Jordan Miles: Thanks Maya, Diego. Bye.

Meeting end.
